mn77:6.5: Those teachers who were thought by people to be capable of leading others across the ‘river’ of saṁsāra (the wandering-on from life to life). See the simile of the cowherd, Sutta 34.
mn77:9.2: Kosa (here translated ‘cupful’) is the name of the fruit of Hydnocarpus anthelmintica, just as bilva is the name of the Indian ‘bael’ fruit. Disciples live on amounts of food equal to these fruits, not on the fruits themselves.
mn77:9.5: This is literally what the Pāli says; possibly the meaning is the very fine fibres of some species of gourd.
mn77:9.11: During the four months of the rains residence, bhikkhus must have a shelter with a roof, four walls, and a door.
mn77:12.5: That is, everything taught by the Buddha arose out of a causal occasion and was taught with reference to mental states, persons, places, and so on.
mn77:12.6: The word translated ‘marvel’ is difficult to render into English; the Dhamma is marvellous because it is meaningful and therefore convincing—two other senses of this word which should be borne in mind.
mn77:14.1: For the expression dukkhotiṇṇo see M.i, 192. ‘I satisfy their minds’: literally, ‘I capture their mind’.
mn77:23.1: Abhibhāyatana—base for transcendence: i.e. for ‘transcendence of defilement’, according to Comy. Often rendered ‘basis of mastery’, which seems, however, both unclear and wide of the point.
mn77:24.1: Also translated as ‘totality’. This is explained at length in Vis. Ch. IV, where it is said that successful kasiṇa contemplation arrives at complete withdrawal of mind from the five-door sensual sphere and concentration exclusively on a single ‘wholeness’ as a mental object. The Eight Liberations, Eight Bases for Transcendence, and Ten Totalities are closely related: liberations 1-2 correspond to the earth/water/fire/air totalities and bases for transcendence 1-4; liberation 3 (or loving-kindness) corresponds to the blue/yellow/red/white totalities and bases for transcendence 5-8; liberation 4 corresponds to the space totality; and the consciousness totality has no corresponding base for transcendence. In the Visuddhimagga the ninth and tenth totalities are replaced by light and limited space; liberations 4-7 are the four formless states, and liberation 8 is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
mn77:34.1: ‘World’ here means universal (i.e. the whole world-system), not merely the earth.
